newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador vice president appointed interim president.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador vice president appointed interim president.

text.p: Ecuador's Vice President Rosalia Arteaga was formally appointed interim president on Sunday, as the Andean nation tried to resolve the political crisis sparked by the ouster of flamboyant leader Abdala Bucaram.

But the 40-year-old Arteaga, Ecuador's first woman president, was likely to serve even less time as head of a caretaker government than Bucaram, whose colourful six months in office ranked among the shortest in the recent history of Latin America's turbulent politics.
Congress was expected to pass new legislation in a few days to allow it to reappoint its leader, Fabian Alarcon, as president, with Arteaga returning to the vice-presidency.
Alarcon, 50, would serve as interim head of state until Aug. 10, 1998, then hand over power to a president chosen in general elections to be held early next year.

In a brief speech at the ornate Carandelet presidential palace, Arteaga, a lawyer and former education minister, said Ecuador "fortunately found a constitutional solution" to a crisis that had put it "on the edge of the abyss."
Apparently acknowledging she would head a brief transitional government, she pledged "to serve my fatherland ... within the time limits that circumstances offer."

The complex deal leading to Arteaga's appointment was hammered out during the night by legislators and Ecuador's powerful military leaders who, political sources said, were unwilling to back any deal that had no legal standing.
In a joint statement released on Sunday, the armed forces and national police reiterated their "unyielding democratic vocation and absolute respect for the Constitution."

Alarcon was initially voted into the presidency by Congress on Thursday after Bucaram was dismissed for mental incompetence, but legal questions arose over the legislators' ability to unilaterally select a replacement president.
The vote plunged Ecuador in political turmoil, with three people, Bucaram, Arteaga and Alarcon claiming the presidency.
Bucaram, not known for giving up easily, finally conceded on Sunday that what he called a military-backed "congressional coup" left him without a mandate but he remained defiant.

In a rambling interview on national television in the middle of the night at his home in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil, he vowed to make a political comeback, saying: "I'm going to be a candidate for the presidency in the next elections."
The 45-year-old populist, who enraged his impoverished nation with economic belt-tightening measures, said Ecuadoreans would soon bitterly regret his dismissal.
"If you think I'm crazy today just wait to see what kind of craziness is coming in the future," Bucaram, who is popularly known as "El Loco" or "madman," told Ecuavisa television.
He maintained that he was a victim of conspiracy and hardball politics Latin-style.
He accused the military high command of allowing Congress to "usurp" power from a sitting president, who was never given the right to defend himself in an impeachment trial.

His embittered remarks, delivered in his traditional abrasive style, followed the resignation of his defence minister on Saturday and a statement from a respected army general confirming that the military had pulled the rug out from under his government.

Bucaram was ousted after a crippling strike shut down most of Ecuador for two days last week. The stoppage was called to protest harsh austerity measures -- including sharp increases in electricity, gas and public transport rates -- ordered in January by the same man who promised in last year's campaign to champion Ecuador's overwhelming majority of poor people.

In a news conference at his home on Sunday, Bucaram predicted Ecuadoreans would demand his return to power within two weeks because the "civilian dictatorship" would shake international confidence in Ecuador's democratic institutions.

"This is a national disgrace and what we've seen here is a coup," he said, adding that he would go to the United Nations, to the Organisation of American States and even to the Vatican to prove his point, "with the Constitution in hand."
